content: The postage-paid form for requesting information can be obtained by calling 800-822-7967 (toll-free). The Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices (ACIP) will periodically review its recommendations as new information becomes available regarding smallpox disease, smallpox vaccines, the risk of smallpox attacks, adverse events related to the vaccine, and the experiences gained from implementing recent recommendations. This supplemental report provides detailed recommendations for the use of the smallpox vaccine in the pre-event vaccination program in the United States. To enhance preparedness and response, smallpox vaccination is recommended for individuals designated by public health authorities to investigate and follow up on initial smallpox cases that may require direct patient contact. ACIP recommends that each state and territory establish and maintain at least one smallpox response team. ACIP and the Healthcare Infection Control Practices Advisory Committee (HICPAC) recommend that acute-care hospitals identify healthcare workers who can be vaccinated and trained to provide direct medical care for the first smallpox patients requiring hospital admission. These workers should also be prepared to evaluate and manage patients suspected of having smallpox. When feasible, the first-stage vaccination program should prioritize previously vaccinated healthcare personnel to reduce the likelihood of adverse events. Additionally, individuals administering the smallpox vaccine in this program should also be vaccinated. The smallpox vaccine is administered using the multiple-puncture technique with a bifurcated needle, which is included in the vaccine kit along with the diluent. For primary vaccination, 2-3 punctures are recommended, while 15 punctures are advised for revaccination. A trace of blood should appear at the vaccination site within 15-20 seconds; if no blood is visible, an additional three insertions should be made using the same needle without reinserting it into the vaccine vial. If no evidence of vaccine take is observed after seven days, the individual may be vaccinated again. Optimal infection-control practices and proper site care are essential to prevent the transmission of vaccinia virus from vaccinated healthcare workers to patients. Healthcare personnel providing direct patient care should keep their vaccination sites covered with gauze combined with a semipermeable membrane dressing to absorb exudates and contain the vaccinia virus, minimizing the risk of transmission. The dressing should also be covered by a layer of clothing. Dressings should be changed frequently to prevent the accumulation of exudates and subsequent maceration. Consistent hand hygiene is the most critical measure in preventing contact transmission. Hospitals should designate staff to assess the dressings of all vaccinated healthcare workers. When feasible, staff responsible for dressing changes for smallpox healthcare teams should also be vaccinated, and all individuals handling dressings should adhere to contact precautions. Routine administrative leave is not required for newly vaccinated healthcare personnel unless they are physically unable to work due to systemic signs and symptoms of illness, have extensive skin lesions that cannot be adequately covered, or are unable to adhere to recommended infection-control precautions. Individuals outside the patient-care setting can keep their vaccination sites covered with a porous dressing, and hand hygiene remains crucial to prevent inadvertent inoculation. The FDA recommends that recipients of the smallpox vaccine refrain from donating blood for 21 days or until the scab has separated. Contacts of vaccinees who inadvertently contract vaccinia should also defer blood donation for 14 days after the resolution of their complications. In the pre-event vaccination program, smallpox vaccination is contraindicated for individuals with a history or presence of eczema or atopic dermatitis, other acute, chronic, or exfoliative skin conditions, conditions associated with immunosuppression, those under one year of age, individuals with severe allergies to any vaccine component, and those who are pregnant or breastfeeding. ACIP does not recommend smallpox vaccination for children and adolescents under 18 years of age during the pre-event vaccination program. Vaccination is also contraindicated for individuals with household contacts who have eczema, atopic dermatitis, other skin conditions, immunosuppression, or are pregnant. Individuals with inflammatory eye diseases requiring steroid treatment should defer vaccination until the condition resolves and the course of therapy is complete. Eczema vaccinatum, a severe form of disseminated vaccinia infection, can occur in individuals with atopic dermatitis and other dermatologic conditions. Potential vaccinees should be screened for a history of atopic dermatitis, eczema, or chronic or recurrent rashes in themselves or household members. Those reporting such conditions should not be vaccinated unless a healthcare provider determines the rash is not eczema or atopic dermatitis. Women of childbearing age should be asked if they are pregnant or intend to become pregnant within the next four weeks. Women who respond positively should not be vaccinated. Any woman who suspects she might be pregnant or desires additional assurance should perform a urine pregnancy test on the day of vaccination. If a pregnant woman is inadvertently vaccinated or becomes pregnant within four weeks of vaccination, she should be counseled accordingly. Smallpox is transmitted from an infected person to another, with the highest risk of transmission occurring during the first 7-10 days after rash onset. Transmission can also occur during the prodromal period, immediately before rash onset, when oral lesions ulcerate and release the virus into oral secretions. Airborne transmission is rare. The greatest risk of infection occurs among household members and close contacts of smallpox patients, particularly those with prolonged face-to-face exposure. Isolation of infected patients, vaccination, and close monitoring of contacts at greatest risk have been shown to interrupt smallpox transmission. The primary strategy for controlling a smallpox outbreak and interrupting disease transmission is surveillance and containment, which includes isolating smallpox cases and vaccinating individuals at risk of contracting the disease. This strategy was instrumental in eradicating smallpox as a naturally occurring disease, even in areas with low vaccination coverage. Depending on the size of the outbreak and available resources, surveillance and containment activities were sometimes supplemented with vaccination of additional individuals in the outbreak area to expand the ring of immune persons and further reduce the chance of secondary transmission. ACIP assumes that the risk of smallpox resulting from a deliberate release by terrorists exists but is low, and the population at risk cannot be determined. These recommendations are based on the assumption that appropriate infection-control measures, including personal protective equipment, will provide a certain level of protection from infection.
